subject: Mathematics
learning_objectives: Collect, organise, and represent data in tabular form
Calculate arithmetic mean (average) of a given data set
Find the mode and median of ungrouped data
Draw and interpret bar graphs, double bar graphs
Construct and read pie charts (circle graphs)
Understand the concept of probability and calculate simple probabilities
Apply data handling concepts to real-life situations including Karnataka-specific contexts
prerequisite_knowledge: Basic understanding of data collection and tally marks from earlier classes
Reading simple bar graphs and pictographs from Class VI
Fractions and their relationship to parts of a whole
Basic arithmetic — addition and division for calculating averages

introduction.why_important: Data is everywhere — cricket scores, weather records, exam results, population figures, election results. Data handling gives us the tools to organise raw information into meaningful summaries (mean, median, mode) and visual representations (bar graphs, pie charts) so we can make sense of the world and take better decisions.
introduction.real_life_relevance: A teacher uses mean scores to understand class performance. A weather department uses data to predict monsoons. An election commission uses data to declare results. A shopkeeper uses sales data to decide what to stock. Every profession uses data — data handling is the mathematics of the information age.
introduction.karnataka_context: Karnataka's state government publishes data on crop production (ragi, rice, sugarcane), rainfall, tiger population counts (Project Tiger census), and school enrolment. The BBMP uses data to plan garbage collection routes in Bengaluru. IPL cricket statistics (Bengaluru's RCB) involve huge amounts of data handled using mean, median, and mode. Karnataka's weather stations record rainfall data daily.
introduction.connection_to_previous_learning: Class VI introduced the idea of collecting data and making basic bar graphs. Class VII extends to three measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode), range, pie charts, and introduces the concept of probability.

characters.name: Mean (Average)
characters.role: The 'fair share' measure — what each person would get if everything was distributed equally. Affected by extreme values.

characters.name: Median
characters.role: The 'middle value' — unaffected by extreme values, best for skewed data. For even number of data: average of two middle values.

characters.name: Mode
characters.role: The 'most popular' value — the one that appears most often. A data set can have no mode, one mode, or multiple modes.

characters.name: Probability
characters.role: The measure of how likely an event is to happen — expressed as a fraction between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain).

plot: The chapter opens by asking: how do we make sense of a large collection of numbers?
It introduces the arithmetic mean (average) as the sum of all values divided by the number of values.
It introduces mode as the most frequently occurring value and median as the middle value when data is arranged in order.
It defines range as the difference between the maximum and minimum values in a data set.
It develops bar graphs and double bar graphs to compare data visually.
It introduces pie charts (circle graphs) — showing data as sectors of a circle, where the whole circle = 360° = 100%.
It introduces probability — the chance of an event occurring. P(event) = Number of favourable outcomes / Total possible outcomes.
The chapter connects all concepts through real-life word problems: exam scores, sports statistics, weather, surveys.
story_summary.moral: Data without organisation is noise; organised data becomes information; information with analysis becomes knowledge. Mean, median, and mode are three different 'lenses' to understand data — each tells a different story.

core_concepts.simple_explanation: Mean = sum of all values ÷ number of values (the average). Median = the middle value when data is arranged in order. Mode = the value that appears most often. Range = maximum − minimum.
core_concepts.detailed_explanation: Arithmetic Mean: Mean = (Sum of all observations) / (Number of observations). If marks are 45, 60, 55, 70, 50: Mean = (45+60+55+70+50)/5 = 280/5 = 56. Mean is affected by extreme (very high or very low) values. Median: Arrange data in ascending order. If n is odd: median = ((n+1)/2)th term. If n is even: median = average of (n/2)th and (n/2+1)th terms. Example (odd, 5 values): 45, 50, 55, 60, 70 → median = 3rd term = 55. Mode: The value that appears most frequently. Example: 3, 5, 3, 7, 3, 5, 8 → mode = 3 (appears 3 times). A data set may have no mode, one mode (unimodal), or more than one mode (bimodal/multimodal). Range: Maximum value − Minimum value. Example: max=70, min=45 → range = 25.
core_concepts.real_life_example: A class of 5 students scored: 40, 60, 65, 70, 90. Mean = 325/5 = 65. Median = 65 (3rd value in order). If one student scored 0 (absent), mean drops to 325/5 — but median wouldn't change much. This shows why median is better for skewed data (like income in a country where a few billionaires raise the mean enormously).
core_concepts.karnataka_example: Karnataka's rainfall (mm) in 6 districts: 1200, 800, 600, 1500, 900, 750. Mean = 5750/6 ≈ 958.3 mm. Arranged: 600, 750, 800, 900, 1200, 1500. Median = (800+900)/2 = 850 mm. Mode = none (all different). Range = 1500−600 = 900 mm. The mean (958) and median (850) tell different stories — the high Kodagu rainfall pulls the mean up.
core_concepts.common_mistakes: For median with even number of values, students forget to average the two middle values. Also, students sometimes report all values as modes when asked — if every value appears only once, there is NO mode. Mean is affected by outliers (extreme values); median is not. Students often confuse which measure to use in which context.
core_concepts.memory_tip: Mean = MATHS (add and divide). Median = MIDDLE (arrange and find centre). Mode = MOST (most frequent). Range = MAX minus MIN. '3 Ms and a R': Mean, Median, Mode, Range.

core_concepts.simple_explanation: A bar graph uses rectangular bars to compare data across categories. A pie chart divides a circle into sectors, where each sector represents a proportion of the total. The whole circle = 360°.
core_concepts.detailed_explanation: Bar Graph: Each bar's height (or length in horizontal bar graphs) represents the value for that category. Double bar graphs compare two sets of data side by side for the same categories. Steps to draw: (1) Draw x and y axes. (2) Mark categories on x-axis, values on y-axis with equal scale. (3) Draw bars of equal width with gaps between them. Pie Chart (Circle Graph): Each sector's angle = (value/total) × 360°. To construct: find each sector's angle, draw circle, mark angles with protractor. Example: if 60 out of 120 students prefer cricket, cricket sector angle = (60/120) × 360° = 180°. Reading pie charts: each sector as fraction of 360° = fraction of total.
core_concepts.real_life_example: A pie chart showing Karnataka's crop production: rice 40%, ragi 30%, sugarcane 20%, others 10%. Rice sector angle = 40/100 × 360° = 144°. Ragi = 108°. This instantly shows rice is the dominant crop without reading numbers.
core_concepts.karnataka_example: Bengaluru's transport mode survey (1000 people): 400 use private vehicles (144°), 300 use public bus (108°), 200 use metro (72°), 100 walk (36°). Total = 360°. A double bar graph comparing Bengaluru and Mysuru cricket match attendance across 5 years would show both cities' data side by side for easy comparison.
core_concepts.common_mistakes: In pie charts, students forget that angles must sum to 360°. Always verify: add all sector angles — if not 360°, there's a calculation error. In bar graphs, students sometimes make bars of different widths — all bars must be equal width. Also, the scale on the y-axis must be uniform (equal intervals).
core_concepts.memory_tip: Pie chart angle = (part/whole) × 360°. The whole pie = 360° = 100% of data. Sector angle proportional to data value. Bar graph: bars show quantity, height = value. Remember: PIE = 360°, BAR = height = value.

core_concepts.simple_explanation: Probability is the measure of how likely an event is to occur. P(event) = Number of favourable outcomes / Total number of possible outcomes. Probability is always between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain).
core_concepts.detailed_explanation: Key terms: Experiment = an action with uncertain outcomes (tossing a coin, rolling a die). Outcome = a single result of an experiment. Event = a set of one or more outcomes. Sample Space = the set of ALL possible outcomes. Formula: P(E) = n(E)/n(S) where n(E) = favourable outcomes, n(S) = total outcomes. Examples: Tossing a coin: S = {H, T}, n(S) = 2. P(Head) = 1/2. Rolling a die: S = {1,2,3,4,5,6}, n(S) = 6. P(getting 4) = 1/6. P(getting even) = 3/6 = 1/2 (even numbers: 2,4,6). Key facts: P(impossible event) = 0. P(certain event) = 1. 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1. P(E) + P(not E) = 1.
core_concepts.real_life_example: Weather forecast: '70% chance of rain tomorrow' = P(rain) = 0.7. Quality control: '5 defective items in 100' → P(defective) = 5/100 = 1/20. Card game: drawing a red card from a standard deck = 26/52 = 1/2.
core_concepts.karnataka_example: At a Dasara lucky draw in Mysuru, 500 tickets are sold, of which 50 are prize winners. P(winning) = 50/500 = 1/10 = 0.1. In a cricket match between Karnataka and Delhi, if Karnataka has won 6 out of 10 past matches, P(Karnataka winning) = 6/10 = 3/5 = 0.6 (based on past data — not a true probability calculation but an estimate).
core_concepts.common_mistakes: Students sometimes give probability > 1 (e.g., writing 8/5). This is IMPOSSIBLE — probability is always between 0 and 1. Also, students confuse favourable outcomes with total outcomes. In P(getting a 3 on a die), favourable = 1 (only the outcome '3'), total = 6.
core_concepts.memory_tip: P(event) = FAVOURABLE / TOTAL. Always a fraction between 0 and 1. P=0 → IMPOSSIBLE. P=1 → CERTAIN. P=½ → EQUALLY LIKELY either way. 'FATE' = Favourable ÷ All Total Events.

key_terms_glossary.meaning: A collection of facts, numbers, or measurements gathered for analysis. Raw data is unorganised; organised data is arranged in a meaningful way (tables, graphs).
The average of a set of values, calculated by dividing the sum of all values by the number of values. Mean = (Sum of observations) / (Number of observations).
The middle value of a data set arranged in ascending (or descending) order. For even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle values.
The value that appears most frequently in a data set. A data set may have no mode, one mode, or multiple modes.
The difference between the maximum and minimum values in a data set. Range = Maximum value − Minimum value. Measures the spread of data.
A graph using rectangular bars of equal width to represent and compare data across different categories. The height (or length) of each bar represents the frequency or value.
A bar graph with two bars per category, used to compare two sets of data simultaneously for the same categories.
A circular graph divided into sectors, where each sector represents a proportion of the total. The full circle = 360°. Sector angle = (value/total) × 360°.
A measure of the likelihood of an event occurring, expressed as a number between 0 and 1. P(E) = Number of favourable outcomes / Total possible outcomes.
The set of all possible outcomes of a probability experiment. For a coin toss: {H, T}. For a die roll: {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.
An outcome that satisfies the conditions of the event being studied. In P(rolling a 6), the favourable outcome is {6} — just one outcome.

worked_examples.question: Find the mean, median, mode, and range of: 4, 7, 2, 9, 7, 3, 7, 5
step_by_step_answer: Step 1 — Mean: Sum = 4+7+2+9+7+3+7+5 = 44. Number of values = 8. Mean = 44/8 = 5.5.
Step 2 — Median: Arrange in order: 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 7, 7, 9. n=8 (even). Middle terms = 4th and 5th = 5 and 7. Median = (5+7)/2 = 6.

worked_examples.question: In a survey of 200 students about their favourite sport: Cricket=80, Football=60, Badminton=40, Others=20. Find the angle for each sector in a pie chart.
A bag contains 5 red, 3 blue, and 2 green marbles. One marble is drawn at random. Find P(red), P(blue), P(green), P(not red).
The mean of 5 numbers is 24. If four of the numbers are 18, 25, 30, 22, find the fifth number.
step_by_step_answer: Mean = Sum / n → Sum = Mean × n = 24 × 5 = 120.

quick_check_questions.after_concept: Data Handling — Mean, Median, Mode, Probability

questions.q: What is the sector angle for a category with 45 values out of a total of 180 in a pie chart?
A die is rolled. Find P(getting a number greater than 4).
When is the median a better measure than the mean?
questions.a: When the data has extreme values (outliers). The mean is pulled by outliers but the median is not. Example: incomes of 5 people: ₹10,000, ₹12,000, ₹11,000, ₹13,000, ₹1,00,00,000. Mean is distorted by the last value; median (₹12,000) better represents the typical income.

key_takeaways: Mean = Sum of all values ÷ Number of values. Affected by extreme (outlier) values.
Median = middle value of ordered data. For even n, average the two middle values. Not affected by outliers.
Mode = most frequently occurring value. Can be none, one, or multiple modes.
Range = Maximum − Minimum. Measures the spread of data.
Bar graph: equal-width bars, height = value, uniform scale on axes.
Double bar graph: two bars per category to compare two data sets.
Pie chart sector angle = (value/total) × 360°. All angles must sum to 360°.
Probability: P(E) = Favourable outcomes / Total outcomes. Always between 0 and 1.
P(impossible event) = 0. P(certain event) = 1. P(E) + P(not E) = 1.
Mean, Median, Mode are three 'measures of central tendency' — each describes data differently.

revision_notes: Chapter 3 — Data Handling. Central Tendency: Mean = Sum/n (affected by outliers). Median = middle value after ordering; even n → average of two middle terms; not affected by outliers. Mode = most frequent value; can be none/one/multiple. Range = Max−Min. Bar graphs: equal bars, uniform scale. Double bar graphs: compare two sets. Pie charts: sector angle = (value/total)×360°; all angles sum to 360°. Probability: P(E) = favourable/total; 0≤P≤1; P(certain)=1; P(impossible)=0; P(E)+P(Ē)=1. Sample space = all possible outcomes. Key formula for finding missing value: if mean and n are known, Sum = Mean×n; missing value = Sum − (sum of known values).
must_remember_facts: Mean = (Sum of all observations) / (Number of observations).
Median: arrange in order. Odd n → middle term. Even n → average of two middle terms.
Mode = most frequently occurring value. No mode if all values appear equally.
Pie chart: sector angle = (value/total) × 360°. Sum of all angles = 360°.
P(E) = Number of favourable outcomes / Total possible outcomes.
Mean is affected by extreme values (outliers); median is not.
If mean of n values = M, then sum of all values = M × n.
